paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, companies judged their employees mainly by output: how many products they made or how many sales they achieved. Only in recent decades have large employers begun to measure how staff feel about their work, often through short online surveys sent every few weeks.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Supporters of these surveys point to a clear link between wellbeing and performance. A study of 1,800 call-centre workers found that in weeks when employees reported being happier, they made more calls per hour and converted more of those calls into sales. The effect was strongest among newer staff.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Critics argue that the surveys themselves can cause harm. If workers suspect that their answers are not anonymous, they may give the responses they think managers want, making the results useless. In one company, scores rose sharply after a manager publicly praised the teams with the highest ratings.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: There is also disagreement about what should be measured. Some surveys ask simply whether people are satisfied, while others ask about specific experiences, such as whether they feel their opinions are heard or whether they have the equipment they need. Researchers generally find the second kind more useful, because the answers suggest what could be changed.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Measuring wellbeing is pointless unless something happens as a result. Employees who complete surveys repeatedly without seeing any response often become more cynical than those who were never asked. For this reason, several consultants recommend that companies share the results with staff and announce at least one change after each survey.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Smaller businesses rarely use formal surveys, relying instead on regular conversations between managers and staff. A recent report suggested that this informal approach can be just as effective, provided managers are trained to listen rather than to defend decisions already made.
paragraphs.label: F
